options: Unsafe, but only because the plain save is a different function. If it ran in the same process as the swap, the lock would stop it.
Safe, because the save runs in a different process and the lock applies per process, so it makes the swap wait until the save finishes.
Safe: the swap holds the exclusive lock, so the OS blocks any other write to the key's file for as long as the lock is held.
Unsafe: the plain save never asks for the lock, so it can write between the swap's check and its write. The swap then returns success and the save's value is silently overwritten.
MultipleChoice.prompt: A file-backed store keeps one JSON document per key in a directory. A compare-and-swap operation takes an exclusive advisory lock on `<dir>/.lock`, reads the document, compares it with the expected value, writes the new one, then releases the lock. A teammate adds a plain `save` operation that just overwrites a document and, because it is not a compare-and-swap, does not take the lock. Two processes then run at the same time: one calls the swap on a key, the other calls `save` on the same key. Is the swap's guarantee that its check and write happen as one step still sound?
reasons: Who is protected does not depend on the process. A save that never requests the lock bypasses it whether it runs in the same process or a different one. What matters is that each writer takes the lock.
This reverses how the lock works. It does not make the swap wait for anything unless the other side also requests the lock. A different process that never requests it is not held off at all.
The lock is advisory. The OS only makes other lock requests wait. It does not stop a process that never asks for the lock from writing, so the plain save goes straight through.

An advisory lock only excludes processes that also try to take it. Because the plain save skips the lock, the swap's check and write are not one step. Every writer of the directory has to take the same lock, not only the ones doing compare-and-set.
